title: Music Fundamentals II: Minor Scales and Key Signatures, Melody, Timbre, Texture

guide.summary: Unit 2 covers minor scales and keys, intervals and their inversions, melodic features, transposition, timbre and instrument families, and musical texture.

sections.heading: Minor scales and keys
sections.body: Natural minor follows W–H–W–W–H–W–W (scale degrees 1 2 ♭3 4 5 ♭6 ♭7). Harmonic minor raises 7 to create a leading tone (A harmonic minor: G♯), producing an augmented second between 6 and 7. Melodic minor raises 6 and 7 ascending (A B C D E F♯ G♯ A) and uses natural minor descending. Relative keys share a key signature (C major / A minor; the relative minor is a minor third below). Parallel keys share a tonic (C major / C minor). In minor, the raised 7 is written as an accidental, not in the key signature.

sections.heading: Intervals
sections.body: Intervals have a number (count letter names) and a quality: perfect (unisons, 4ths, 5ths, octaves), major or minor (2nds, 3rds, 6ths, 7ths), augmented or diminished. In a major scale, intervals above the tonic are major or perfect. Inversions: numbers sum to nine (3rd ↔ 6th), major ↔ minor, augmented ↔ diminished, perfect stays perfect. The tritone (augmented 4th or diminished 5th) spans three whole steps. Consonances: perfect unison, octave, fifth, and major/minor thirds and sixths; the perfect fourth is dissonant above the bass in common-practice harmony.

sections.heading: Melody, transposition, timbre, texture
sections.body: Melodies may be conjunct (stepwise) or disjunct (leaps); they have range, contour, and climax, and are built from motives and sequences. Transposing instruments sound at a different pitch than written: B♭ clarinet and B♭ trumpet sound a major second lower; F horn sounds a perfect fifth lower; E♭ alto saxophone sounds a major sixth lower. Timbre is tone color (instrument families: strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion). Texture: monophony (single line), homophony (melody with accompaniment or chordal), polyphony (independent lines, e.g., imitation in a fugue), heterophony (simultaneous variants of one melody).

sections.heading: Worked example: intervals
sections.body: To name an interval, count letter names for the number, then determine quality. C up to E is a third; since E is in C major, it is a major third. C up to E♭ is a minor third. C up to G♯ is an augmented fifth, and C up to G♭ a diminished fifth. To check, count half steps: a major third has four, a minor third three, a perfect fifth seven, and a tritone six. For intervals above notes other than C, think of the major scale on the lower note: if the upper note is in that scale, the interval is major or perfect.

sections.heading: Minor in practice
sections.body: In minor-key melodies, listen for the raised seventh at cadences, which creates the leading tone. In harmonic minor, the step between lowered 6 and raised 7 is an augmented second, often avoided in vocal melodies by using melodic minor. When writing minor scales, add accidentals for raised degrees rather than changing the key signature.

sections.heading: Texture and timbre on the exam
sections.body: Aural questions may ask you to identify instruments, voice types, or textures. Monophony is a single unaccompanied line; homophony is melody with chordal accompaniment; polyphony has independent lines, often with imitation; heterophony has simultaneous variations of one melody. Identify instrument families by timbre: bright brass, reedy woodwinds, warm strings, and percussive keyboards.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students mislabel intervals by counting half steps but not letter names, transpose in the wrong direction, and forget raised degrees in minor.

sections.heading: Worked example: transposition
sections.body: To transpose a melody for B♭ clarinet, write it a major second higher than concert pitch, so a concert C becomes a written D. For F horn, write a perfect fifth higher: concert C becomes written G. For E♭ alto saxophone, write a major sixth higher: concert C becomes written A. Remember to change the key signature too: a melody in concert F major becomes G major for B♭ clarinet.

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know relative and parallel keys, harmonic and melodic minor, interval quality, inversion, tritone, conjunct and disjunct motion, timbre, and texture types.

keyTakeaways: Relative = same signature; parallel = same tonic.
Interval inversions sum to 9; M↔m, A↔d.
B♭ instruments sound M2 lower; F horn P5 lower.
commonMistakes: Putting G♯ in the A minor key signature.
Counting half steps but mislabeling interval numbers.
examTips: Count letter names first, then quality.
Listen for the raised leading tone in minor.
Identify texture by counting independent lines.

a. G harmonic minor: G A B♭ C D E♭ F♯ G.
b. D melodic minor ascending: D E F G A B C♯ D.
c. E♭ up to C is a major sixth.
d. Its inversion is a minor third.
